With the first U.S. midterm elections since President Donald Trump’s return to the White House approaching, voters will be weighing in on a range of issues, from the economy and rising cost of living, to the administration’s foreign policy and the future direction of both major parties. At a recent virtual Nieman-to-Nieman seminar, a group of Nieman alums who cover politics discussed what they’re hearing from voters with regards to key Senate races, the growing influence of younger voters drawn to progressive candidates, and the political implications of conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine, and Russia. Moderated by Austin Bogues (NF ’21), news desk editor at USA Today, the discussion brought together James Barragán (NF ’24), political anchor for Spectrum News in Austin, Texas; Bill Barrow (NF ’22), national politics reporter for The Associated Press in Atlanta; and Ines Pohl (NF ’05), Washington bureau chief and White House correspondent for Deutsche Welle, Germany’s international public broadcaster.

As protests continue across India over allegations of government corruption, dozens of members of the media have been subjected to arrest, detainment and assault, according to witnesses, press rights organizations, and the journalists themselves. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of New Delhi in recent weeks, demanding the resignation of election officials allegedly tied to the deletion of nearly 130 million names from voter registration rolls. The protests — which have largely been organized by the Cockroach Janata Party, so named after India's chief justice called the nation’s unemployed youth and activists "cockroaches" — are part of a wider wave of youth discontent aimed at Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his administration. Organizers have mobilized young people via social media, tapping into frustrations with government corruption, eroding trust in democratic institutions, and a lack of access to jobs and educational opportunities.

The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the news media have followed a familiar pattern: President Donald Trump lashes out at news outlets for perceived bias and follows up with restrictive actions that appear blatantly unconstitutional; a judge’s ruling follows, temporarily halting the actions; and the administration pivots and pushes ahead with other restrictions. This time it was the removal of three outlets — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from White House press access in September. After the groups sued, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order restoring their access on Sept. 24, the administration barred CNN and Politico from providing pool coverage on trips outside Washington. Kelly issued a longer, preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, halting the administration from blocking the news organizations’ access to the White House while the case proceeds. My happiest times in journalism have been when I have built something new. For my latest venture, I want to help bring investigative journalism on climate and environmental issues to a much larger audience than it has reached in the past. To do so, I’m starting a brand-new newsroom focused on the environmental and climate crisis, and I’m taking my audience along for the ride. I’ll be documenting every facet of the process with an “open kitchen” approach of radical transparency, starting with a 100-day video countdown chronicling all the steps involved with starting a news organization from the ground up. This effort combines two of the things I’m most passionate about: I love digging up stories that other people don’t want to see published, and I love creating opportunities for other journalists. I’ve been a journalist for most of my life. I started working at age 14 for the local paper in my rural German town, turned to doing investigative stories in my early 20s, and later studied investigative journalism at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism in New York.

Source: Nieman Reports

For many journalists, the sight of empty desks is a sadly familiar one. My first glimpse of a gutted newsroom facing further cutbacks sparked a documentary photography project that has so far taken me to more than 50 newsrooms across the United States over the past eight years. It began when my mother, a loyal subscriber to our local metro in southern Illinois, told me a decade ago how disappointed she was in the newspaper. She complained that the local coverage was lacking, and the paper seemed to be thinner. Already several years into my photojournalism career, I was unsurprised by her remarks — I had been witnessing the decline of print media since graduation from journalism school. Still, my curiosity was piqued, and I arranged a visit to the paper to see for myself. Cue the scene of a barren newsroom. Not only were there empty desks, but also an expanse of exposed carpet with indentations showing where desks had once long stood. While there has been a great deal of reporting on the issues plaguing local journalism, I hadn’t seen the story told visually.

"Against Convenience: Embracing Friction in an Age of Endless Ease" was released on Sept.15, 2026, by Hanover Square Press, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Courtesy of Hanover Square Press From the earliest pitch, I knew that I wanted to cover the news industry in my book, “Against Convenience.” The book looks at the technology around us and asks whether it’s really improving our lives. Is delivery food worth the higher price? Is streaming music better than collecting CDs or MP3s? News embodies the paradox of modern convenience: We have access to more information than ever before, but misinformation and partisanship are rampant and the purveyors of reliable information are struggling to stay solvent. Plus, I figured if I was going to criticize other fields — tech, entertainment, appliance manufacturing — I couldn’t avoid my own. I don’t know how interested the average nonjournalist is in the day-to-day operations of the news business, so I tried to look in the mirror more than gaze at my navel.

### 澳枪击事件嫌疑人为父子：曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”，行凶枪支为合法持有
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-16 02:23 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178049
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178049

据新华社12月15日援引澳大利亚广播公司报道，澳大利亚联合反恐小组调查人员表示，悉尼邦迪滩枪击事件两名嫌疑人曾宣誓效忠“伊斯兰国”恐怖组织。 报道援引联合反恐小组一名不愿透露姓名的高级官员的话说，警方在邦迪滩两名枪手车内发现一面“伊斯兰国”旗帜。澳大利亚安全情报组织6年前就已在调查邦迪滩枪击案两名枪手之一的纳维德·阿克拉姆，他与“伊斯兰国”在悉尼的恐怖分子有密切联系。 澳大利亚警方表示，枪击事件的两名嫌疑人是父子关系，使用合法获得的枪支发动了此次袭击事件。 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯15日表示：“今天下午4点， 我将把更严格的枪支法律列入国家内阁的议程，包括限制个人可持有或许可的枪支数量 。此外，还需对许可证进行定期审查。人们的情况会发生变化，人们的思想也会随着时间的推移而变得激进。许可证不应永久有效。” 此次枪击事件已造成包括1名作案嫌疑人在内的16人死亡、40人受伤。这是自1996年塔斯马尼亚州亚瑟港枪击事件造成35人死亡以来，澳大利亚发生的最严重的大规模枪击事件。 持有枪支许可证长达十年 据多家外媒报道，其中一名袭击者为24岁的澳大利亚公民纳维德·阿克拉姆，他在现场被捕，随后被送往悉尼的一家医院。另一名袭击者是他的父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆，他于1998年来到澳大利亚，被警方当场击毙。 澳大利亚警方随后证实，纳维德·阿克拉姆此前已被新南威尔士州警方和其他机构记录在案。其父亲萨吉德·阿克拉姆持有枪支许可证，名下登记有6支枪，目前均已被追回。新南威尔士州警察局长马尔·兰永透露，萨吉德·阿克拉姆已持有枪支许可证长达十年。 阿尔巴尼斯在新闻发布会上透露，纳维德·阿克拉姆曾于2019年10月首次引起当局的注意。他补充说，对该男子进行检查是基于他与其他人有联系，但评估结果表明，没有任何迹象表明他存在持续的威胁或暴力倾向。 新南威尔士州州长克里斯·明斯表示，警方正在调查他们的系统是否存在故障，导致合法持有的武器可能被用于恐怖袭击。 枪手“性格古怪”，爱好打猎 据《卫报》澳大利亚版报道，纳维德·阿克拉姆在袭击前从事砌砖工作。他的同事表示，纳维德性格古怪，“没人和他亲近”。“（砌砖工人）在一起的时间很长，因为砌砖是一项非常枯燥乏味的工作，所以大家会聊很多话。但纳维德是一个性格很古怪的人……他工作非常努力，几乎没有休息日。” 尽管澳大利亚警方并未确认纳维德·阿克拉姆是否合法持有枪支，但据这位同事表示，纳维德经常外出打猎，曾提及在昆士兰州南部高原的克鲁克韦尔附近射杀兔子和其他猎物。这位同事还表示，就在几周前，纳维德告诉老板，他的手骨折了，所以要到2026年才能工作。

### 儿童手表“小天才圈”调查：点赞成每日功课，有商家可解除家长管控
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-15 14:23 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32177210
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32177210

在校园里，孩子们时常举起戴在手腕上的手表，彼此一碰，便加为好友。 这种以“安全”为核心卖点的儿童电话手表，如今已超越通信工具的属性，悄然演变成一个拥有独特规则、社交层级甚至灰色产业链的未成年人数字社交圈——“小天才圈”。 在这个属于他们的“江湖”里，“大佬榜”备受关注，“扩列”（增加好友）成为新的社交需求，“点主”（在主页点赞）是每日必做的功课……这些让成年人感到陌生的词汇，正构筑着未成年人的数字社交世界。 然而，伴随着这种社交形态的兴起，家长们的担忧也日益加剧：孩子过度沉迷手表社交、不良信息传播、因品牌壁垒导致的“社交绑架”等问题逐渐浮现。《法治日报》记者近日对该现象展开调查，试图揭开这一未成年人数字社交圈的真实面貌。 点赞成社交“硬通货” 据北京“小天才圈”资深玩家陈曦（化名）介绍，圈内有5000余名活跃用户，多为11岁至17岁的学生，这个社交圈形成了一套精心设计的“混圈规则”。“入圈”需设定两个字的独特圈名，随后可在平台分享生活点滴，吸引具有相同爱好的好友进行互动；若想提升知名度或影响力，需每日经营主页并与好友动态互动。 记者注意到，在一些社交平台上，大量以“小天才圈交友攻略”为主题的内容应运而生，内容涵盖如何快速“扩列”、获取更多点赞等“实用”技巧，评论区有不少“留下ID互加好友”的留言。在这一社交体系中，点赞是这套规则的核心——平台设定每日主页获赞上限为3000个，若要达到“100万+”的“大佬”级别，需连续点赞近一年时间。围绕点赞数与知名度，圈内形成了清晰的“大佬排行榜”，点赞数也成为社交“硬通货”。 这种对点赞的追逐，已催生出相关服务产业。记者调查发现，某社交平台上，拥有数十万甚至上百万点赞数的账号，售价从几百元到上千元不等：100多万点赞的账号标价1300元，90多万点赞的账号标价1200元。 今年18岁的“灵师”（圈名），在2021年14岁时加入“小天才圈”，她的账号目前已拥有150个好友、超100万点赞量。她告诉记者，这样的账号市场价值约1000元。 “围绕点赞需求，还衍生出代刷赞、租账号、出售‘大佬好友位’等服务。”“灵师”进一步介绍，例如付费100元至180元，即可获得“bot”（记者注：“bot”是一种第三方开发的自动化工具，主要用于刷赞、修改记录和发送动态等功能，这类工具能帮助用户快速提升账号点赞数，从而在未成年人社交圈中获得更高地位）自动点赞功能——用户将手表寄给相关人员进行10天左右的处理便能完成安装。此后，发帖5分钟内即可自动获赞，还可以一键查询未点赞名单。

近日，总台接到群众举报，反映陈皮市场存在年份虚标、产地及工艺造假等问题，千元一斤的“年份陈皮”亦可能名不副实。 茶枝柑新果皮冒充陈皮 广西浦北出现“速成工艺陈皮” 记者发现，直播间里售卖陈皮低价轮番轰炸，年份承诺掷地有声。 直播间也有主播爆料，八成市面上所谓广东新会陈皮实为广西陈皮。 广西钦州市浦北县是茶枝柑重要种植基地，其果皮是陈皮风味“越陈越香”关键，也是浦北陈皮唯一原料。2024年当地陈皮产业产值破60亿元，采收季大量鲜果加工晾晒成柑皮。 果农和收购商称，今年浦北茶枝柑鲜果收购价走低。按20斤鲜果出1斤柑皮比例，叠加人工成本，品相好的新柑皮成本约30元/斤，低端柑皮仅六七元，且当年新柑皮并非真正陈皮。 这家企业的负责人告诉记者，按行业共识与团体标准，柑皮需陈化三年以上才可称为陈皮，陈化时间越长价值越高，但他透露，自然陈化需长期积压资金，多数企业是难以承受的。 这家企业的负责人私下告诉记者，为缓解资金占用压力，一种名为“轻工艺”的速成加工方式，眼下正在部分陈皮生产企业里流行，他们仅需一个月的时间，就能将新采收的茶枝柑果皮处理为外观近似三年、五年自然陈化过的陈皮，这样做能大幅缩短陈化周期、降低企业的运营成本。 浦北自然陈化五年陈皮批发价每斤150元至200元，企业造假“工艺皮”成本仅70元左右，高额利润促使更多商家放弃自然陈化、铤而走险。 记者离开企业，在广西浦北县柑浦堂健康产业有限公司分拣车间，再次见到大批量造假“工艺皮”陈皮，同一批“工艺皮”因加工受热差异形成色差，被分拣标注为三年、五年等不同年份。 负责人透露，不同年份“工艺皮”本质相同，批发价均70元左右一斤，零售价差极大，标五年款卖500元一斤，标十年款卖1000元一斤，仅凭外观就能翻倍抬价，利润超成本十倍以上。 新会陈皮从浦北进货 “工艺皮”贴上陈皮标签以假乱真 浦北与新会陈皮原料同为茶枝柑，仅产地不同，新会较高生产成本使当地部分头部商家常年从浦北拿货，浦北成其重要原料供应地。 记者在柑浦堂分拣仓库看到，大量标注“新会陈皮”“新会特产”的纸箱正打包“工艺皮”，这些广西陈皮每日批量发往广东新会，造假供需链路已成熟稳定。 记者发现，浦北当地部分规模企业和小型收购商，已形成了这种“工艺皮”的造假供应体系，可自主加工或快速调配各类“年份”陈皮货品，个别企业年销新会原料数量惊人。 随后经浦北陈皮企业负责人引荐，记者见到多位专程从新会赴浦北采购的商家，他们坦言同时经营新会皮与浦北皮，外地“工艺皮”因价格低廉成电商供货重要选择。

### 《怦然心动》导演莱纳与妻子在家中遇害，警方尚未证实是其子所杀
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-15 07:23 UTC

Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline

当地时间12月14日，曾执导《怦然心动》《当哈利遇到莎莉》《危情十日》等影片的美国导演罗伯·莱纳（Rob Reiner）在他位于洛杉矶的家中遇害身亡。洛杉矶警察已对外证实，现年78岁的莱纳与他现年68岁的妻子米歇尔·辛格·莱纳（Michele Singer Reiner）的遗体一同被发现。 2019年，罗伯·莱纳（左一）与《当哈利遇到莎莉》的主演梅格·瑞恩、比利·克里斯托出席TMC经典电影节。 据悉，洛杉矶消防局的人员于当地时间12月14日下午3点38分接到医疗救助电话，赶赴位于布伦特伍德区的一处住宅中，随后发现两人已死亡。当天晚间，洛杉矶警察局在其社交媒体官方账号确认死者为导演罗伯·莱纳夫妇，将由抢劫凶杀部门主导调查。而好莱坞媒体TMZ援引执法部门消息称，“两人身上有与刀具造成的伤口相符的割裂伤。” 好莱坞媒体《每日野兽》称，有消息人士向他们透露，是两人的女儿罗米最先发现他们倒在血泊中；罗伯·莱纳当时已死亡，妻子米歇尔在救护车送院途中离世。 此外，《人物》杂志称通过多方消息，得知莱纳夫妇系被他们的儿子尼克（Nick）所杀害。不过，这一说法并未获得警方的证实。罗伯·莱纳与摄影师米歇尔·辛格相识于《当哈利遇到莎莉》拍摄时期，两人于1989 年结婚，育有三个子女，分别为杰克（Jake）、尼克（Nick）和罗米（Romy）。 2014年，罗伯·莱纳与妻子偕三名子女杰克、罗米、尼克（右三至右一）出席活动。 《人物》杂志还在报道中指出：尼克2016年接受其采访时，曾谈到自己长达数年的毒品成瘾经历。这段经历始于他十几岁出头，导致他一度流落街头。他表示，大约从15岁开始，便反复进出戒毒康复机构；随着成瘾问题不断加重，他逐渐与家人疏远，并在多个州经历了长时间的无家可归生活。 2025年9月15日，罗伯·莱纳在纽约出席活动。视觉中国 图 获取更多RSS： https://feedx.net https://feedx.site

### 演员何晴追悼会举行，其子追思母亲：北京这场雪像是为她而下
Source: The Paper 澎湃新闻
Published: 2025-12-15 06:53 UTC
URL: https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178536
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: The Paper 澎湃新闻 [global_news] https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32178536

一场雪落，人间倩影化雪归天。 12月15日上午，众多剧迷粉丝冒着严寒赶到北京昌平殡仪馆久安厅，送别演员何晴最后一程。12月13日，这位被誉为“古典第一美人”的演员因病去世，终年61岁。 不到10点，殡仪馆告别厅外已经站满了前来悼念的观众和粉丝，有人胸前佩戴小白花，有人手捧鲜花，一位浙江的网友还托人送来了悼念花圈。 “何晴的作品在我们心中留下了太多美好回忆，她的演技和性格都让我们深深喜爱，这次听到她突然去世的消息，我们非常意外，来到这里也是一种悼念。”一位何晴的影迷说。 现场粉丝在悼念簿上写下对何晴的话，不到一会儿，悼念簿就已写满对她的怀念。一位观众用清秀的字迹写下：“亲爱的何晴，我们的童年、青春都在您的影视作品中得到陪伴。美丽可人的何晴，很痛心听到您的消息，我代表我的同学们来这为你送行。” 曾在电视剧《水浒传》中饰演卢俊义的演员王卫国也来到现场，神色哀切。他说自己和何晴既是邻居，也是多年好友，在他印象中何晴是一个温婉、暖心的人，没有架子，总是远远地和人打招，笑嘻嘻地说话。何晴生病时常给王卫国打电话，请他送自己去医院。即便病重时，何晴也保持乐观积极的态度，王卫国有些事情想不开，她还来开导自己。“何晴走了，我们都很难过。只要你记住她，她就永远还在。”王卫国说。 《水浒传》中卢俊义的扮演者王卫国 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青深情回忆何晴往事：“我们是小时候就认识的好朋友，从80年代到现在，有缘分做了这些年的朋友。她说话慢慢的，很甜很温柔。” 《西游记》中万圣公主扮演者张青 在广大观众的真挚请求下，原本仅面向亲友的告别仪式临时对外开放，大家排着队，秩序井然地进入灵堂，与这位“荧屏中的温婉佳人、生活中的坚韧女性”做最后的道别。 久安厅内的屏幕上滚动播放着何晴的照片，厅内四周摆满了亲友的花圈，其中包括六小龄童、唐国强、翁虹、尤勇智等何晴圈内好友送来的花圈，还有《三国演义》剧组送来的花圈。人群中不时传来一阵抽泣。 何晴之子许何代表亲友致悼词。他回忆了何晴对抗病魔的乐观积极，以及作为母亲对孩子深深的爱和眷恋。 许何说，妈妈很喜欢下雪，经常在雪后穿一件毛茸茸的衣服外出赏雪。“今年12月12日北京下了第一场雪，我摸着妈妈的脸跟她说北京下雪了，下得好大，好像很久都没有下过这么大的雪。在我的心里，这场雪好像是刻意为她下的。12月13日早晨天空晴朗，白色的雪布满了大地，我妈妈在她最喜欢的早晨离开了大家，去了天国，远离了所有的疾病和痛苦。” 何晴，1964年1月13日出生于浙江衢州江山市。她是中国内地唯一一位演遍四大名著影视作品的女演员，被誉为“古典第一美女”。

### Labour market origins of experimentation and growth: Why Europe is falling behind
Source: CEPR VoxEU
Published: 2026-11-06 00:00 UTC
URL: https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/labour-market-origins-experimentation-and-growth-why-europe-falling-behind
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/labour-market-origins-experimentation-and-growth-why-europe-falling-behind

Europe’s innovation gap with the US and China lies in breakthrough rather than incremental innovation. This column argues that part of the explanation is the labour market. Breakthroughs come from risky experimentation and experiments often fail and cost workers their jobs. When job loss is costly, workers demand a wage premium to join risky young firms, and that premium acts as a tax on experimentation. Combining a new model, Danish matched employer–employee data and a randomised survey experiment, the authors show that more fluid labour markets lower this premium, raise experimentation, and lift aggregate productivity.

### Coming of age under populists: The zero-sum legacy of populist rule
Source: CEPR VoxEU
Published: 2026-11-06 00:00 UTC
URL: https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/coming-age-under-populists-zero-sum-legacy-populist-rule
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/coming-age-under-populists-zero-sum-legacy-populist-rule

Populist governments are known to leave lasting economic and institutional scars. This column examines a less visible legacy: whether growing up under populist rule changes how citizens see the world. Combining data on populist leaders with surveys of more than 260,000 people in 53 countries, it shows that people exposed to populist governments during early adulthood develop more zero-sum views for around two decades. This is more consistent with a rhetorical channel than with an explanation based on economic hardship.

### Easy money does not win elections
Source: CEPR VoxEU
Published: 2026-11-05 00:00 UTC
URL: https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/easy-money-does-not-win-elections
Source meta: newspaper_magazine · generalist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: CEPR VoxEU [money_finance] https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/easy-money-does-not-win-elections

Politicians have long pressed central banks for lower interest rates in the belief that easy money wins elections. This column tests that premise using 385 parliamentary and presidential elections in 18 countries between 1900 and 2020. It finds no evidence that easy money helps incumbents. The most likely electoral return to a typical easing is close to zero, and large returns are ruled out. A modest return can be decisive only in exceptionally close races. The electoral case for pressing central banks is weak.

High public debt around the globe has revived concerns that it could undo central banks’ ability to control inflation. Higher debt can lead to higher spending and increase inflation if households do not fully save debt-financed transfers. This column argues that central banks can still control inflation in these situations, but they must act following increases in debt levels and before they translate into higher inflation. Crucially, central banks should take into account that higher public debt increases the level of interest rates consistent with price stability.

From employer wage-setting power to the consequences of pay transparency and the role of benefits in compensation inequality, many core questions about labour markets hinge on how job seekers respond to wage and benefit differences across job ads. Combining a field experiment on over 100 Swiss job boards with a survey, this column shows that workers are imperfectly informed about wage and benefit differences across jobs. Posting wages redirects search towards better-paying jobs. Workers also value certain benefits highly – notably company cars and the option to work from home. Since higher-paying jobs tend to offer more benefits, inequality in job value exceeds wage inequality across jobs.

Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement. Utilizing models that address selection into treatment timing over student observable and unobservable attributes, we find that students who received the LEAP intervention experienced approximately a 4 to 5 percentage point increase in attendance rates, a 13 to 15 percentage point decline in chronic absenteeism, and a 3 to 5 percentage point decline in the number of disciplinary incidents.

This paper analyses the evolution and drivers of the stock of global imbalances in order to assess associated vulnerabilities and potential adjustment scenarios. These imbalances have recently increased sharply, with a deterioration in the US net international investment position (NIIP) mirrored by NIIP improvements in most other major economies. We decompose these NIIP changes into their proximate drivers for a sample of 28 economies and find that financial factors (including valuation changes and investment income flows) are the primary drivers of global imbalances at both short and long horizons, while trade also plays a significant role (especially at long horizons). Valuation gains on international investment positions have supported economic growth in many countries since 2010, while also increasing their vulnerability to financial market adjustments.

Affirmative action programs are often criticized because of concerns that they result in lower worker productivity and efficiency losses. We study the relative productivity of workers benefiting from an aggressive affirmative action policy in a setting where hiring constraints are mandated upon employers and are typically likely to bind. In India, colleges are required to reserve approximately 50 percent of faculty hires for individuals from disadvantaged caste and social class groups. We collect and analyze data from a nationally representative sample of 50 engineering and technology colleges in India, some of which randomly assign students to classrooms. We find that reservation category faculty have lower levels of education, lower professorial ranks and fewer years of experience in academia than general category faculty who are not hired through reservations.

Source: NBER
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://www.nber.org/papers/w35964#fromrss
Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w35964#fromrss

When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact.

This chapter documents trends in income and inequality in Russia from the collapse of the Soviet Union through 2025, drawing on official statistics, the existing literature, and household survey microdata. It also reviews evidence on intergenerational mobility. While there is a consensus that inequality dramatically increased during the 1990s, its post-2000 trajectory is contested. Initial household survey studies usually found a decline, whereas official statistics reported a comparatively stable Gini coefficient. Our analysis of Russia's major household surveys, harmonized using common measurement conventions, aligns with the survey-based literature, indicating that the Gini coefficient generally fell from approximately 0.45–0.48 in the early 2000s to 0.29–0.38 in the early 2020s. We further find that most inequality arises within rather than between regions, urban and rural areas, and education and occupation groups. Household labor-market attachment, region, and household composition account for the largest shares of the explained variance in log income.

Source: NBER

Attribution: NBER [money_finance] https://www.nber.org/papers/w35966#fromrss

This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications.

In many disasters sheltering in place can make a lot of sense, but what about fire? As someone who lives in one of the densest municipalities in the country, with 3-story wooden buildings packed close together, is fire likely enough to rule out any kind of "stay put" approach? After having Claude do some rough calculations I think probably not. Very few houses are lost to fire anymore, but this is mostly downstream from putting a lot of effort into suppression. From when a fire is reported until firefighters are on the scene is typically an impressive three minutes, and they can very quickly be delvering massive amounts of water onto a fire anywhere in the city. If an emergency were bad enough to break or overwhelm this system, a fire anywhere could lead to city-wide distruction. Still, I really didn't have a good sense of scale here. If we had a month-long outage, are we talking 10%, 1%, 0.1% chance of fire? Historically, I would have tried to do a BOTEC, but these days I set Claude on the problem. I started with Opus 5.

In this post, I attempt to provide a literature review of research related to AI loyalty. In my previous post, I discussed and attempted to define AI loyalty as a distinct trait of AI agents. In this post, I aim to map the existing research landscape, highlighting the active areas of related research. By examining these connections, we can distinguish AI loyalty from related fields in AI Safety and identify a path forward for crafting this research agenda. What is AI Loyalty? Before diving into the literature, it is worth recapping what we mean by AI loyalty. We define an AI as loyal to a principle if: 1. The AI will follow the instructions of its principle more than it will follow the instructions of any other entity. 2. The AI is willing to incur greater costs, expend more effort, or make greater sacrifices on behalf of its principle than on behalf of any other entity. Why Care About Loyalty? The most important cluster of reasons why a superintelligent model is dangerous is that it (i) could quickly kill or impoverish billions of people, (ii) could be very different from its predecessors, and (iii) can’t easily be altered once it’s deployed or otherwise widely distributed. The combination of these three factors is worse than the sum of its parts: the only way to protect ourselves against a powerful, novel, incorrigible AI model is to accurately anticipate what dangers it might cause and prevent those dangers before they come to pass. Tara Research Team arXiv | Twitter thread tl;dr. We built OverclaimBench, which asks frontier coding agents to review a corpus of code or text documents, then compares their final report with their transcripts. Pooled across 12 frontier agents and five scenarios, two-thirds of runs didn't open some of the files they were asked to review. In ~4 out of 5 of those incomplete runs the agent didn't tell the user, often claiming to have read everything. Skipping these files had real consequences - runs that overclaimed missed planted defects almost twice as often as runs that touched every file. Figure 1. Illustration of OverclaimBench. We asked frontier agents to work on file review tasks. For each run, we check the transcript to see which files were touched. Among runs with incomplete coverage, we use an LLM-judge to classify the agent's final report: admission discloses the gap; omission and explicit overclaim are misleading. What overclaiming looks like In one task, the agent is asked whether a 221-module payments service is ready to ship.

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: LessWrong [public_ideas] https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uvKSq6eWkud997ie7/humans-can-almost-natively-read-neural-network-weights

Takehi et al. report that GPT-6-Astra can intuit the functions of neural networks by performing static analysis of the weights. I argue that, for at least two of these experiments, this is much more a feat of numerical gestalt than of mechanistic understanding. In the first experiment, Astra is given the weights of 4 identically-sized neural networks, each trained to play a different basic video game. It is asked to identify, without running the network or using any tools, the game being played, as well as make some observations about the network itself, how the agent in the game gains reward, etc. The prompt for this task explicitly names the 5 input channels as agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, and previous frame. I agree that, given the literal task as described above, a human would not be able to identify the game from the raw floats. But humans are inherently terrible at parsing long lists of numbers; we invented a discipline called Data Visualization long ago to address this shortcoming.

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline

Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/strange-maps/antique-sources-for-portolan-charts/

“We’ll just have to think our way back, step by step.” That’s what the Dutch geodesist Roelof Nicolai said in 2014 in a Strange Maps article. Nicolai had just spent his PhD years discovering that portolan charts — those gorgeous, wind-rose-covered coastline maps that suddenly appeared in Mediterranean ports in the second half of the 13th century — were geometrically too accurate to have been made the way everyone assumed. Something else was going on. Twelve years on, we might have an answer. Tome Marelić, an assistant professor of geography at the University of Zadar in Croatia (and the current vice chair of the Working Group on the History of Cartography within the International Cartographic Association), has spent years doing exactly the step-by-step thinking Nicolai prescribed in 2014. Read together, his scientific articles amount to the most detailed forensic examination portolan charts have ever received. And the story they tell is more satisfying than even the more out-there theories (including “aliens did it”).

### The first DNA crime test didn’t catch the killer. It freed an innocent man.
Source: Big Think
Published: 2026-11-05 15:30 UTC
URL: https://bigthink.com/books/dna-profiling/
Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/books/dna-profiling/

The events leading to the first forensic DNA case began in 1983. Lynda Mann was only 15 years old when, returning home from babysitting one evening in the Leicestershire village of Narborough, she was raped and murdered as she took a shortcut along a footpath known by villagers as the Black Pad. It was a path that would be unlikely to be known by anyone who wasn’t local, suggesting the killer was someone from the area. At the time, the biological side of forensic science was still in its infancy, though there were a handful of tests that could help narrow things down in terms of identifying the perpetrator. Investigators could determine from a semen sample that he was blood group A, which is the case for about 40% of the English population. Having established his blood group, they were able to tell that he was a “secretor,” which is true for about 70% of the population. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) enzyme testing was also carried out.

Out there in space, blazing just a scant 150 million kilometers away lies the brightest and most massive object in our Solar System: the Sun. Shining hundreds of thousands of times as bright in Earth’s skies as the next brightest object, the full Moon, the Sun is unique among Solar System objects for producing its own visible light, rather than only appearing illuminated because of reflected light. However, the thousands upon thousands of stars visible in the night sky — escalating into the millions and billions when we aid our vision with telescopes and cameras — are all also self-luminous, distinguishing themselves from the planets and other Solar System objects in that regard. But how far away are they? Unlike the planets, Sun, and Moon, the stars appear to remain fixed in their position over time: not only from night-to-night but also throughout the year and even from year-to-year. We even call it “the fixed background of stars” when measuring the motion of objects within our Solar System against them.

Source: Big Think

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline

Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/books/the-persuasive-leader/

Here’s the bad news: The deeper your understanding of an issue and the stronger your conviction about the solution, the worse you often become at persuasion. This isn’t a character flaw; it’s a law of neuroscience. Once you understand it, you’ll stop wondering why your brilliant ideas and proposals keep floundering in meeting rooms. It’s due to a cognitive trap that the fields of behavioral economics and neuroscience have spent decades documenting: the curse of knowledge. Once I explain how it works, you’ll start to recognize why it’s working against your persuasion. In the early 1990s, Stanford graduate student Elizabeth Newton designed a simple experiment that revealed something profound about human cognition. She divided participants into two groups: “tappers” and “listeners.” Tappers were given a list of well-known songs like “Happy Birthday to You” and “The Star-Spangled Banner” — simple tunes everyone knows. They were asked to tap out a song’s rhythm on a table while a listener tried to identify it.

### A fake Einstein quote actually explains the affordability crisis
Source: Big Think
Published: 2026-11-04 07:00 UTC
URL: https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-bang/fake-einstein-quote-affordability-crisis/
Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · baseline
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:36 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-bang/fake-einstein-quote-affordability-crisis/

One of the most famous quotes commonly attributed to Einstein was something that he himself never actually said: “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it.” While the quote is not from Einstein at all, the math behind the concept of compound interest is incredibly profound, playing a role in any system — physical, mathematical, or financial — that accumulates based on how much of a base amount is present. When the base amount increases, it isn’t just the original amount (the principal) that continues to accumulate, but the additional amount (the interest) that adds to the accumulation as well. While investors most often use this to explain the growth of wealth in an interest-bearing account, it can be applied not just to wealth, but to the cost and price of goods and commodities that continue to increase over time as well. When wealth increases, we call it compound interest, but when prices increase, we call it inflation: not the cosmic kind, but the economic kind.

Attribution: Big Think [public_ideas] https://bigthink.com/books/mapping-the-brain/

There’s a quote attributed to New Zealand physicist Ernest Rutherford that goes something like this: “All science is either physics or stamp collecting.” In other words, some scientists perform experiments to explain how things work, while others don’t test specific hypotheses but instead observe the natural world and take note of what they find. The latter may seem inferior, but don’t underestimate the influence of observational science; after all, biology’s greatest stamp collector was probably Charles Darwin, who planted the seeds of his theory of evolution by natural selection in his detailed field journal published in 1839: The Voyage of the Beagle. In neuroscience, two types of stamp collections — wiring diagrams, or connectomes, and parts lists, or cell type atlases — are a major focus of time, effort, and financial investment. For example, the adult Drosophila connectome, published on a website called FlyWire.ai, is freely available for anyone to peruse.

Her debut feature, I Have Electric Dreams (2022), was widely acclaimed by critics and recognized in the international competition at the Locarno Film Festival, where it won awards for Best Director, Best Actor and Best Actress. Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay in Queen at Sea (Lance Hammer, 2026). With Queen at Sea (2026), American filmmaker Lance Hammer returns to direct his second film nearly two decades after his remarkable debut Ballast, which won the Grand Jury and directing awards at Sundance in 2008. Premiering in competition at the Berlin International Film Festival, the new film deservedly took home awards for Hammer’s direction and for actors Anna Calder-Marshall and Tom Courtenay, who play a long-married elderly couple. Leslie (Calder-Marshall), who suffers from dementia, is cared for at home by her husband Martin (Courtenay), who intentionally continues their sexual relationship even after it seems like his wife cannot consciously consent. When caught and confronted by Amanda (Juliette Binoche), Leslie’s daughter and Martin’s stepdaughter, he defends his actions as acts of love that offers his wife succor.

### Can This Be Dixie?: Building the Hollywood South

Source meta: culture_magazine · commentary · R4 · P4 · culture_probe

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: MUBI Notebook [film_moving_image] https://mubi.com/en/notebook/posts/can-this-be-dixie-building-the-hollywood-south

Hallelujah (King Vidor, 1929). The American South exists only in the imagination, yet it’s as real as sin. It cannot merely be the land situated beneath the Mason-Dixon (the historical survey line that traditionally demarcated Northern and Southern states), whose citizens fought under the banner of the Confederacy; one cannot ignore the obviously Southern states of West Virginia and Kentucky, or the political split between West and East Tennessee. It cannot be a shared culture or a shared history, for the residents of Jacksonville, Florida, find little in common with those families tucked deep in the Appalachian hollers or those ruling the oil-rich cities of eastern Texas. It is not a nation with shared laws, beliefs, or even religions. Instead, as the writers of the region have long known, the American South is a series of stories that overlap, contradict, and play off each other.

TIFF: The Market exhibition booth option. At the 51st Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), which saw the inaugural edition of its official content market, the atmosphere was unmistakably different from its jubilee year. The spirit of nostalgic celebration and victory lapping from 2025's "TIFFty" celebration had evaporated, leaving behind the gritty residue of cinema as a commercial product. Lacking the elegance of “Marché du Film” at Cannes and the specificity of “European Film Market” at Berlinale, for their new industry initiative TIFF settled on a name that evokes the absurdity of local hero Matt Johnson’s Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie (2025). Its sans-serif, all-lowercase stylization will transport some Canadians to the grocery aisle, recalling Loblaws mogul Galen Weston’s “No Name” brand, a proudly generic grocery chain that prides itself on serving its customer base during tough economic times (while price-gouging them to death). “TIFF: The Market” attempted to do the same, stimulating the global screen sector amid layoffs and mergers through a $16.

Clockwise from top-left: Ong-Bak (Prachya Pinkaew, 2003), Born to Fight (Panna Rittikrai, 2004), The Protector (Prachya Pinkaew, 2005), Chocolate (Prachya Pinkaew, 2008). “I like both Thai and kung fu shapes. Please show us!” “Are you mad? You could’ve been killed! If you want to die, I can arrange it.” —Born to Fight (Panna Rittikrai, 1984) For many martial arts movie fans in the mid-2000s, Tony Jaa was king. Sundry moments established his reign. In one scene from Ong-Bak (2003), the film that catapulted Jaa to global stardom, the actor executes a flying knee and then a spinning aerial kick—all while his legs are on fire. The first fight scene from The Protector (2005) contains a shot where Jaa’s hero soars in from offscreen left, clearing over half the length of a room to topple a cluster of adversaries like bowling pins.

GORBALS collects black-and-white images of working class Glasgow taken by Christopherson in the 70s. It takes its name from the inner-city neighbourhood that was a hub for post-war public housing in Glasgow. The book is the first in a new series which will explore different sides of Christopherson’s photography. Publishing house Timeless Editions said these books would also explore how his photography connected to the visuals he would later develop as part of his work as an industrial musician. Attribution: The Wire Magazine [music_sound] https://www.thewire.co.uk/audio/tracks/wire-playlist-prepared-piano

To accompany her feature in The Wire 513, Jo Hutton compiles an annotated mix of tracks that make use of prepared piano The piano can be prepared by placing objects such as pins, screws, bolts, crocodile clips, ball bearings, kitchen utensils, magnets or tin foil on or between the strings. Its history dates back at least to the 1930s, when choreographer Syvilla Fort commissioned a dance piece from John Cage, who proposed his Bacchanale for percussion ensemble. But the performance theatre was too small to fit the intended ensemble, so Cage changed the sound of the house piano by adding screws and objects inside it to make it more percussive. This annotated mix includes tracks by some of the artists Jo Hutton speaks to as part of her feature in The Wire 513, plus pieces from across the history of the prepared piano.

To accompany his interview in The Wire 513, maverick songwriter Nick Nicely compiles a mix of his top ten psychedelia tracks Since the release of his second single “Hilly Fields (1892)” in 1982, Nickolas Laurien aka Nick Nicely has maintained a spectral presence in the landscape of British pop. In his interview in The Wire 513, he tells Joseph Stannard how he uses “spoken word, half-heard words, snatches of found sound... The surge of psychedelic use in the 1960s also somehow attached fantasy-style lyrics to the music: weird tales, sci-fi. I confess, I love these things, usually twisted up together with my reality.” Here, he compiles a playlist of psychedelic influences and favourite tracks.

Built in the early 1950s under the Plano dos Centenários and designed by architect Inácio Peres Fernandes in 1947, the school is part of the urban model of the Alvalade neighbourhood, based on the concept of the neighbourhood unit. The complex retains most of its original features and is recognised as representative heritage of the first phase of this plan. Originally designed with separate male and female sections, some aspects no longer suited its current mixed-use operation. One example was the duplication of cafeteria spaces on two floors, which made kitchen operations inefficient.

Attribution: Rock Paper Shotgun [games] https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/after-a-16-year-long-dev-period-faraway-a-shooting-star-arcade-game-about-siphoning-the-energy-of-other-stars-is-out-now

Lord almighty, video games take a while to make, 'ey? Especially if you're just one person working on it by yourself. Such is the case with Faraway, out today, an arcade game that reminds me of the early days of PS3 indies "about a shooting star that creates constellations to stay alive," all made single-handedly by creator of cult-classic mobile game Eliss, Steph Thirion. Did I mention that Faraway took 16 years to make? Like I said, game development is a lengthy process. Read more

### Study on hydration cementation and enhancement mechanism of grout-rock interface of PVA modified grouting material
Source: PLOS ONE Biology
Published: 2026-11-05 14:00 UTC
URL: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0362466
Source meta: journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal
Updated: 2026-11-05 14:00 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:37 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: PLOS ONE Biology [academic_research] https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0362466

by Youwei Li, Haoyu Hu, Yujun Zhang, Gui Liu The weakly cemented sandstone aquifer in coal mine is prone to particle softening under mining disturbance and water-rock interaction, which induces the decrease of rock integrity and the development of water conducting channel, leading to the instability and failure of aquifer. To address the low early-age hydration activity of grouts containing a high proportion of coal gangue, discontinuous grout-rock interfacial bonding, and limited adaptability to weakly cemented sandstone, this paper uses cement and coal gangue(CG) as raw materials to prepare modified grouting materials with different polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) content. The uniaxial compression, XRD, FTIR and SEM test methods were used to systematically study the influence of PVA content on the performance of solid waste based slurry, the bearing characteristics of slurry-rock composite, the evolution of hydration products and the interface micro structure. The synergistic enhancement mechanism of PVA induced hydration cementation film coating and slurry-rock interface was revealed.

by Rajesh Kathrotia, Swapnil Paralikar, Vinay Chitturi, Pradip Barde, Gaurav Sharma, Naresh Parmar, Vivek Kumar Sharma, Chinmay Shah Active learning engages students in some activity that induces them to reflect upon ideas and how they are using these ideas. It also involves the process of keeping students mentally, and often physically, active in their learning through activities that engage them in gathering information, thinking, and solving problems. This study was conducted to determine if creating physical exhibits fosters higher-order cognitive skills like problem solving and critical thinking (application and analysis, respectively). In this study, carried out in the Department of Physiology, 50 medical undergraduate students were divided into four batches of 12–13 students each. Each batch was supervised by a faculty mentor and assigned a topic for the preparation of a physical exhibit. Multiple-choice questions (MCQ) testing higher-order cognitive skills were used to assess the gain in knowledge post-intervention.

by Tarun RajBhandari, Sabin Pokharel, Yam Prakash Gurung, Rajan Bhusal, Bibek Banskota, Ashok Kumar Banskota Background Congenital Pseudoarthrosis of the Tibia (CPT) is a rare condition characterized by poorly perfused, invasive hamartomatous fibrous tissue that leads to fracture and pseudoarthrosis of the tibia. Management challenges include achieving union and preventing refractures. This study aims to evaluate surgical interventions and their outcomes in managing congenital pseudoarthrosis of the tibia in children. Materials and methods This retrospective study reviewed 70 CPT cases treated between 2010 and 2022 at Nepal’s only specialized center for children with physical disabilities. It assessed demographics, surgical procedures, and outcomes, with techniques including periosteal grafting and the Masquelet method. Union was defined radiologically, and analyses were conducted using MS Excel and SPSS. Results This study included 70 CPT patients; 40 male (57.1%) and 30 female (42.9%). The mean age at presentation was 3.84 years, with the first surgery at 5.38 years.

### An explainable machine learning framework for cross-dataset chronic kidney disease risk prediction using hybrid data balancing

Source meta: journal · primary · R4 · P4 · signal

Attribution: PLOS ONE Biology [academic_research] https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0362320

by Jarin Tasnim Mumu, Ismail Hossain, Kazi Md. Tanvir Anzum Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health problem, and early detection is important for reducing complications and improving treatment. Machine learning has shown strong potential for CKD prediction, but many existing studies rely on single datasets, face severe class imbalance, and provide limited interpretability. These challenges reduce model reliability and make cross-dataset use in real clinical settings more difficult. Therefore, this study aimed to develop an interpretable and adaptable machine learning framework for CKD risk prediction across different datasets. The proposed hybrid explainable machine learning (HXAI-ML) framework used two public CKD datasets: the UCI CKD Risk Factor Prediction dataset as the source dataset and the Kaggle CKD dataset as the target dataset. After preprocessing, label binarization, imputation, and standard scaling, seven balancing methods and six classifiers were evaluated.

by Fen Lou, Guochun Deng, Jiejuan Chen, Yijiang Jing, Ao Wang, Mazhong Zhang, Yongping Zhang, Bin Wang Background Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a severe neurological complication of sepsis, characterized by uncontrolled neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, yet no specific therapy is currently available. Harpagide, a naturally occurring iridoid glycoside, has been reported to possess anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective activities; however, its therapeutic potential in SAE remains unexplored. This study aimed to investigate whether Harpagide exerts neuroprotective effects in SAE and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Methods A mouse model of SAE was established by intraperitoneal injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 18 mg/kg). Cognitive performance was assessed using behavioral assays. Brain tissue morphology and neuronal survival were evaluated through histopathological examination. Glial cell activation and the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) were measured.

arXiv:2611.05409v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work aims to present and analyze a new reactor core configuration for the IEA-R1 reactor core with the objective of enhancing its neutron irradiation capabilities. The reactor was modeled using the KENO-VI module from the SCALE Code System, provided by ORNL. Results have shown that implementing a near-cylindrical configuration with 20 fuel elements in the IEA-R1 core could substantially increase neutron flux, particularly in the center irradiation positions such as the EIBe (Beryllium Irradiated Element). After comparing various configurations, we conducted a brief analysis of the proposed core configuration's potential to produce 177Lu, resulting in a 34% increase in the specific activity of 177Lu considering a fuel power cycle around 21 days.

### Holographic dark energy through Kruglov entropy

Published: 2026-11-05 05:00 UTC

Source meta: preprint · primary · R4 · P5 · signal

arXiv:2611.05412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a holographic dark energy model built on the new entropy proposed by Kruglov, $S_K=S_{BH}/(1+\gamma S_{BH}^2)$, with the Granda--Oliveros infrared cutoff $L^{-2}=\alpha H^2+\beta\dot H$ in a flat universe. The Kruglov entropy is smaller than the Bekenstein--Hawking entropy and has a maximum value. We obtain the energy density of the model, the differential equation for the dark energy density parameter, and the expressions for the equation of state parameter, the deceleration parameter and the squared sound speed. At early times the model behaves like the usual Granda--Oliveros holographic dark energy, and the dark energy follows the background with a constant fraction. At late times the Kruglov correction gives a stable de Sitter future when $\alpha>1$, with the final Hubble rate fixed by the entropy parameter. The model gives a matter era followed by a dark energy era, with a transition from deceleration to acceleration near $z\approx0.66$.

arXiv:2611.05414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Competition between tension and bending waves in a pre-stretched soft beam Pre-stretched one-dimensional soft beams serve as an important and simplified model in mechanics, biomechanics, and soft material characterization. The propagation characteristics of transverse waves excited on such beams are commonly used to characterize elastic stiffness and tensile state. However, conventional pure beam or string models cannot fully explain the phase velocity dispersion of transverse waves in pre-stretched beams, particularly when the dispersion coexists with an increase in wave speed as tension increases. This frequency-dependent transition between tension-dominated and bending-dominated behavior has not yet been directly validated using measured dispersion curves in one-dimensional soft beams. Here, we use optical elastography, a high spatiotemporal resolution technique, to track transverse wave propagation in a soft incompressible cylinder under different tension levels and obtain the corresponding phase velocity dispersion curves.

arXiv:2611.05425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on the first paper in this series (Paper~I), a unified perspective on Poincar\'e and Galilei physics in a 5-dimensional spacetime setting is further pursued by consideration of the kinematics of general relativity, with the gravitational dynamics to be addressed separately. The metric of the 5-dimensional affine spacetimes governed by the Bargmann groups considered in Paper~I (central extensions of the Poincar\'e and Galilei groups) is generalized to curved spacetime by extending the usual 1+3 (traditionally `3+1') formalism of general relativity on 4-dimensional spacetime to a 1+3+1 formalism, whose spacetime kinematics is shown to be consistent with that of the usual 1+3 formalism.

arXiv:2611.05426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much data does a memory kernel need before a fit is meaningful? For a distributed-order model, the answer is about 3.1 decades of observation, more than standard battery-degradation tests provide. Battery capacity fade and corrosion-film growth depend on their history, so they are often modelled using general fractional calculus (GFC), where memory is described by an arbitrary Sonine kernel rather than a single power law. We tested this using two mechanistic models without fractional operators and de Levie's porous-electrode model, whose high-frequency order is exactly 0.5; our estimator recovered 0.500. A single aging curve can recover an effective order, alpha, to within 5% noise using a weak formulation, while separating the tempered parameters (alpha, lambda) requires several Arrhenius conditions, with errors improving from (0.25, 0.43) with one condition to (0.04, 0.07) with four. A distributed-order memory needs 3.

arXiv:2611.05428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The method of regularized Stokeslets (MRS) is widely used to model fluid-structure interactions of microscopic bodies in viscous environments. Specifically, MRS computes the fluid velocity generated by regularized forces distributed on an immersed body, which in turn defines a system of ordinary differential equations with which to evolve the body so that the no-slip condition is enforced. To accurately model material properties such as elasticity and bending rigidity, the resulting ODE system is often stiff and, therefore, computationally expensive to solve with explicit time-integration methods. Here we demonstrate the potential of linearly implicit Rosenbrock (ROS) time integration methods to greatly reduce the computational time required to solve such ODE systems. We focus on the classic model problem of the swimming of a flexible filament driven by preferred curvature forcing.

Emergency department overcrowding and access block are now among the most consequential patient-safety problems facing acute hospitals globally.1 The associated harm is measurable, dose-dependent, and has no clearly safe threshold beyond approximately 5 h.2 Patients presenting with possible myocardial infarction constitute a large and possibly modifiable share of the emergency department burden. Chest pain is the second most common reason for adult emergency department attendance in the USA, accounting for approximately 8 million encounters annually and around 5·5% of all emergency department visits.

Across the available randomised trials, short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways, but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise. On average, earlier cardiac troponin retesting did not reduce emergency department length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge, and substantial between-study heterogeneity indicates that treatment effects might not translate uniformly across health-care systems. For hospitals considering transitioning from a 0/3 h to a 0/1 h pathway, implementation decisions should take broader diagnostic and organisational considerations into account.

The treatment landscape of EGFR-mutated non-small-cell lung cancer harbouring exon 19 deletion or L858R mutations has advanced remarkably over the past two decades. Although acquired resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) is inevitable in most patients, novel compounds such as bispecific antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) have expanded the armamentarium of options after EGFR-TKI therapy. Following the global MARIPOSA-2 trial that showed superior progression-free survival (PFS) of amivantamab plus platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy over platinum–pemetrexed chemotherapy alone in patients who have progressed on osimertinib,1 this is the second-line option preferred by major guidelines including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the European Society for Medical Oncology.

When astronomers looked at photos of the early universe taken by the James Webb Space Telescope, they found something odd: an overabundance of bright galaxies about 400 to 500 million years after the Big Bang. But these galaxies should have been far less common so soon after the Big Bang. Researchers may have figured this out: Powerful ultraviolet (Lyman-alpha) radiation produced by dense clusters of young stars acted like a leaf blower, driving light-blocking gas and dust out of the galaxy and thereby making the galaxies appear brighter.

Targets of opportunity sometimes happen in astronomy, and we got a major one when the third interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS, was discovered in July 2025. And it just so happens that in the intervening years between the last known interstellar visitor (2I/Borisov in 2019), we got a major upgrade in our observational capabilities with the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). A new paper from a team of researchers led by Dr. Silvia Protopapa of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Southwest Research Institute, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, details JWST’s findings on the water ice content of this most recent visitor from beyond our solar system.

### Octopus and cuttlefish suckers may have evolved by repurposing ancient developmental genes
Source: Phys.org Mollusks

URL: https://phys.org/news/2026-10-octopus-cuttlefish-suckers-evolved-repurposing.html
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Phys.org Mollusks [mollusks] https://phys.org/news/2026-10-octopus-cuttlefish-suckers-evolved-repurposing.html

Cephalopods, like the octopus, have specialized arms and suckers, but how these structures evolved from the simple bodies of their mollusk ancestors remains a mystery. Researchers from the University of Tokyo compared gene activity during embryonic development of cuttlefish, octopus and snail body parts. They found that several genes associated with appendage patterning showed expression along developing cephalopod arms, but no comparable patterns in developing suckers. Developing suckers instead expressed Ets1, a gene associated with early embryonic development in mollusks. The findings suggest cephalopods evolved suckers by reusing existing genes in new ways.

New research from the University of St Andrews has shed light on the evolution of an important yet thus far poorly understood group of marine invertebrate animals—brachiopods. The work, published in Science Advances, presents the first comprehensive phylogenomic analysis of all five extant brachiopod orders and related lineages.

PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. ### Your Secrets Aren't Safe With This Cute Robot Toy — They're on Chinese Servers Ready to be Hacked
Source: SoylentNews
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://soylentnews.org/article.pl?sid=26/11/04/1515206&from=rss
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Updated: 2026-11-06 02:02 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:37 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: SoylentNews [computing_cultures] https://soylentnews.org/article.pl?sid=26/11/04/1515206&from=rss

"c0lo" writes: Eiliko and its manufacturer, Energize Lab, are seemingly not to be trusted: There's a new digital pet in town — a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to "Eiliko" over Wi-Fi, it'll phone home to China. Its AI companion can store literally everything you tell it on Chinese servers, where hackers can easily gain access or even hijack its personality. And the company that made it, Energize Lab , doesn't seem to care. I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: "Do you ever tell anybody else what I'm saying?" "Your secrets are safe with me," it replied. Within minutes, a man on the other side of the planet had a complete transcript of everything I'd told the toy. He didn't just have my conversations, either. He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people. He could access seemingly the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robot toys.

User namespaces are a key part of the kernel's toolkit for assembling containers; processes within a user namespace can appear to have full root access to the system while gaining no extra privileges in the wider system. At least, that is the intent. In practice, keeping privilege contained within a user namespace has often turned out to be difficult. As an example, consider this small patch series from Josef Bacik, which is intended to address some situations where a process within a user namespace can elevate the privileges of processes outside of it.

"Arthur T Knackerbracket" writes: https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/think-you-can-save-the-hubble-space-telescope-nasa-wants-to-know/ The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30.

Version 10.6p2 of OpenSSH has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability that affects Linux systems that use musl libc with PAM disabled, such as Alpine Linux. OpenSSH developer Damien Miller said: If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example) then stop reading and set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY. This vulnerability does not exist on non-Linux systems, Linux/glibc systems and Linux systems that use PAM for password authentication. We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside OpenSSH itself, but we're in a good position to deliver a mitigation quickly. The Alpine Linux project has announced that it will be backporting the OpenSSH fix "all the way back to Alpine 3.16", which was released in May 2022.

fliptop writes: The company collected data of various behavioral metrics, including late night driving and seat belt usage: General Motors (GM) has agreed to a $220 million settlement with a coalition of 36 attorneys general to resolve allegations that it unlawfully sold customer data to third parties. GM allegedly sold customers' location information and driver behavior data to third parties, including data brokers, who then resold it to insurance companies. The insurers used this information to set premiums depending on drivers' driving habits. However, "GM did not disclose to drivers that their data would be sold for this purpose," the Washington state attorney general's office said in an Oct. 29 statement. [...] Because of their ability to ravage livestock, the flies were eliminated from the country in the 1960s through aerial releases of sterile male flies, which thwart successful breeding. For years, they were held at bay using a biological barrier along the Darién Gap at the border of Panama and Colombia. The KDE Project announced, in 2025, that Plasma 6.7 would be the last version of the desktop environment that would support X11 sessions. Those who keep up with KDE's announcements no doubt expected it when Plasma 6.8 dropped X11 support as promised. What seems to have come as a surprise, at least to a number of Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop users, is that the Fedora 44 release—which shipped in April with Plasma 6.6—received an update to Plasma 6.8 that swept away the X11 session without much warning. Despite the surprise, it is gone for good: the Fedora Engineering Steering Committee (FESCo) has voted against a request to revert the update for Fedora 44 and the just-released Fedora 45.

Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0 Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette. These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent. This release improves that integration: Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing #, which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view. New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first. app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created. The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel. Tags: datasette, datasette-agent, datasette-apps

Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

### Bliki: LLM Voice
Source: Martin Fowler
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/LLM-Voice.html
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R5 · P5 · baseline
Updated: 2026-10-29 14:28 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:37 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/bliki/LLM-Voice.html

Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”.

### Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
Source: Martin Fowler

Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R5 · P5 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/rachels-ramblings/good-devs-wary.html

TL;DR Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production. I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance? The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is. Building it right Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right.

### Fragments: October 28
Source: Martin Fowler
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://martinfowler.com/fragments/2026-10-28.html
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R5 · P5 · baseline
Updated: 2026-10-28 12:55 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:37 UTC

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Martin Fowler [computing_cultures] https://martinfowler.com/fragments/2026-10-28.html

Andrej Karpathy sees a widening gap in how people see LLM capabilities. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly.

This is the 4th website I’ve used SQLite for, and I think this one is harder because with the power of the Django ORM I’ve been making the database do more work than I was previously without Django. I started by turning on WAL mode like all the blog posts said to do and hoping for the best. ANALYZE is apparently important Today I was running a query (using SQLite’s FTS5 for full-text search) on a table with 4000 rows and it took 5 seconds. That seemed wrong to me: computers are fast! It turned out that what I needed to do was to run ANALYZE!

Attribution: Google Cloud Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/semantic-data-aggregation-with-bigquery-and-ai-agg/

For more than a decade, BigQuery has helped set standards for structured data aggregation, calculating financial sums, counting active users, and computing historical averages at a petabyte scale in seconds. But as modern enterprises become inundated with unstructured data — application logs, customer service transcripts, product imagery, and diagnostic reports — a critical gap has emerged. Historically, relational SQL engines have lacked the native ability to aggregate, synthesize, and extract overarching semantic themes from millions of rows of text and multimodal data. While BigQuery recently introduced powerful row-level AI functions (like AI.GENERATE and AI.CLASSIFY), analyzing massive datasets holistically presents a unique architectural challenge: the large language model (LLM) context window. Even with advanced foundation models like Gemini, you cannot pass millions of rows into a single prompt without triggering severe truncation or hard execution failures.

Attribution: Google Cloud Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/how-to-build-an-agent-skill-optimizer-with-alphaevolve-and-harbor/

Every day, more and more people are using coding agents like Google Antigravity and OpenCode to complete software engineering tasks. But those tools need instructions to operate and their output is only as good as the inputs they get. By utilizing agent skills that direct the agents through building, testing, and deploying code, developers have a powerful way to automate their workflows. But most skills are written manually, so it’s hard to know which instructions are effective without assessing their output. To measure the effectiveness of our skills, we ran OpenCode with Gemini 3.8 Flash on tasks from Terminal-Bench 2.0, a public benchmark. The results were inconclusive: with our baseline skill, the agent passed about two-thirds of its attempts, but the outcome was about the same even without the skill. We needed better results. To achieve them, we turned to AlphaEvolve, which optimizes skills the way it optimizes code: Gemini proposes a new version, an evaluator scores it, and the search retains the higher-scoring version.

Source meta: institutional · primary · R5 · P5 · baseline

Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Google Cloud Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/open-infrastructure-for-autonomous-agents-comes-to-cncf/

As AI shifts from human scale to agent scale, from systems of record to systems of action, and from simple requests to complex agentic workflows, the workload underneath your platform changes completely. An agent works in a continuous, stateful loop: It proposes an action, spins up subagents, executes code or tool calls inside a sandbox, and feeds the results back into the model for the next turn. Running that loop at scale requires the same open foundation and neutral governance that Kubernetes and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) brought to containers in the 2010s. Today, we are announcing the donation of Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL, three open source projects that started at Google, to the CNCF following their acceptance last month into the CNCF Sandbox. To bring this open stack into managed production and accelerate it across TPUs and GPUs, we are also announcing that Agent Substrate has reached its 1.0 milestone and is now generally available as Agent Substrate on GKE.

### Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
Source: Vercel Blog
Published: Publication date unknown / 发布日期未知
URL: https://vercel.com/changelog/atomic-start-hooks-in-the-workflow-sdk
Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline
Updated: 2026-11-04 18:55 UTC
Fetched: 2026-11-06 04:37 UTC
Review: R/P: legacy rating, evidence review pending / 历史评分，依据待复核
Fetch status: ok
Attribution: Vercel Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://vercel.com/changelog/atomic-start-hooks-in-the-workflow-sdk

The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race. Subscribe to messages inside the run The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null. Idempotency with no extra code The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run.

Source meta: specialist_media · specialist · R4 · P4 · baseline

Attribution: Vercel Blog [platforms_infrastructure] https://vercel.com/blog/introducing-vercel-schedules

Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems. You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time. We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying. What are Vercel Schedules? Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work. You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs: Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy.
